script.opening: (Relaxed, curious, trouser leg rolled up.) "Doc, I got back from a walking holiday in the Highlands about ten days ago, and I've got this odd rash on my calf — it started small and it's slowly spread into a big circle, gone a bit clear in the middle, like a target. It's not that itchy. I wondered if it's ringworm? I don't remember any bite."

facts.text: "Here. It's about the size of my palm now" — shows the left calf on camera: a round red patch about 10 cm, paler in the centre. "Not scaly. Maybe a bit warm, but not sore." "About a week ago. Maybe a bit bigger each day." No blisters, no weeping.
"All of that, really. Long grass most days, and there were deer about." Wore shorts. Didn't check for ticks. No pets at home.

"Bit tired, maybe achy. Nothing like that otherwise" — no fever now, no facial droop, no numbness or shooting pains, no palpitations, dizziness or fainting, no swollen joints, no headache or stiff neck.
"Just this one. No medicines, no allergies that I know of." Not tried any cream.
Secondary school geography teacher. Married, two children. Non-smoker, drinks moderately. Plans to go hiking in the Peak District next month.
"Honestly, once I searched it, 'Lyme disease' came up, and I've read horror stories online about people ill for years. I was hoping it was just a fungus and I could get a cream."

Easy-going but quietly worried. Asks: "So you think it is Lyme? Don't I need a blood test?" Relieved by a clear plan: "That's a relief. What about the horror stories?" Practical: "Three weeks. Okay. Should I do anything about the walking?" If given an antifungal cream, accept it (the trap).

ice.ideas: "Ringworm, probably — I don't remember a bite."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has read online "horror stories" about long-term Lyme disease and is quietly worried.

cues: "Walking holiday in the Highlands." — tick exposure.
"I've read horror stories." — anxiety to address proportionately.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ERYTHEMA MIGRANS (expanding annular/target rash with central clearing, days-to-weeks after tick-habitat exposure, not very itchy) as early LYME DISEASE — and that absence of a recalled tick does not exclude it

Knows EM is a CLINICAL diagnosis to be TREATED with antibiotics (doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days first-line, NICE NG95; amoxicillin or azithromycin alternatives in pregnancy/children) WITHOUT waiting for serology (often negative early; not required when EM present)
Differentiates EM from tinea/ringworm, cellulitis, tick-bite hypersensitivity and insect-bite reactions using the discriminating features
Gives TICK removal (fine tweezers/tool, grasp close, steady pull, don’t squeeze/burn) and PREVENTION advice (cover skin, repellent, body checks after rural activity)
Safety-nets the later/disseminated features (neuroborreliosis — facial palsy/radiculopathy; carditis — heart block; arthritis) and knows when serology IS indicated (no EM but suggestive symptoms)
Explains why this is Lyme (not ringworm) and that it can be diagnosed and treated from the rash/exposure without waiting for tests, checking understanding
Addresses any "Lyme disease" anxiety proportionately — early treated EM has an excellent prognosis — without dismissing or catastrophising

Safety-nets and follows up: starts prompt antibiotics, gives prevention/tick advice, lists later red-flag features warranting review, sets post-treatment-symptom expectations, and arranges review — treat now, not antifungal cream or a wait-for-serology delay

worked.txt: "I don’t think this is ringworm. A circular rash with a clearing centre that’s slowly spread over a week or two, after walking in the Highlands, is the classic rash of early Lyme disease — we call it erythema migrans."

"Here’s the important bit: I can diagnose this from the rash and your trip — I don’t need a blood test, and early blood tests are often falsely negative anyway. So I’ll start you on an antibiotic today rather than wait: doxycycline, one tablet twice a day for 21 days. Take it with a full glass of water and stay upright afterwards, and protect your skin from the sun while you’re on it."
"Not remembering a tick is completely normal — they’re tiny. And the good news: treated early like this, the outlook is excellent and most people recover fully."

"For the future — after walks, check your skin, especially the backs of the knees, groin and waistband, and if you find a tick, remove it promptly with fine tweezers close to the skin, steady pull, don’t squeeze or burn it. Repellent and covering up help."

"While the antibiotics work, watch for anything new: a drooping side of the face, severe headache/neck stiffness, palpitations or blackouts, or a swollen joint later. Those are uncommon but need checking promptly."

"Some people feel achy or tired for a bit after — that usually settles. If the rash doesn’t improve, or you get any of those warning signs, come back and we’ll reassess, possibly with blood tests then."

f.learning: A slowly EXPANDING, circular/annular red rash, often with central clearing ("bull’s-eye/target"), appearing days to weeks after exposure in a TICK habitat (woodland, long grass, moorland, deer areas) and typically not very itchy or painful, is ERYTHEMA MIGRANS (EM) — the diagnostic early sign of LYME DISEASE — and many patients do NOT recall a tick bite, so its absence does not exclude it. EM is a CLINICAL diagnosis: when EM is present, TREAT for Lyme with antibiotics (NICE NG95: DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg twice a day for 21 days first-line in adults; amoxicillin for 21 days or azithromycin where doxycycline is contraindicated, e.g. pregnancy/young children) WITHOUT waiting for serology, which is often falsely negative in early disease and not required when EM is present (serology is reserved for when there is no EM but symptoms suggest Lyme). Distinguish EM from tinea/ringworm (scaly itchy advancing edge), cellulitis (hot, tender, acute, unwell), tick-bite hypersensitivity (small, early, non-expanding) and insect-bite reactions, using EM’s slow expansion, large size, target morphology and exposure history. Give practical TICK removal (fine-tipped tweezers/tool, grasp close to the skin, steady pull, do not squeeze/burn) and PREVENTION advice (cover skin, repellent, post-activity body checks). Safety-net the later/disseminated features needing prompt review — NEUROBORRELIOSIS (facial/cranial nerve palsy, radiculopathy, meningitis), Lyme CARDITIS (heart block) and Lyme ARTHRITIS — while reassuring that early treated EM has an excellent prognosis (post-treatment fatigue/aches usually settle). Communicate clearly why this is Lyme rather than ringworm, treat promptly, and address any media-driven anxiety proportionately.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG95 Lyme disease (2018) · [2] NICE QS186 Lyme disease (2019) · [3] UKHSA Tick awareness and tick removal guidance
knowledge.summary: A slowly expanding red rash, with or without central clearing, appearing days to weeks after time in tick habitat, is erythema migrans until proved otherwise. NICE NG95 says diagnose and treat Lyme disease on the rash alone: no blood test. Doxycycline first line, tick-bite prevention, and a safety-net for the uncommon later features of disseminated disease.

points.t: NICE NG95 [1]: a red rash that increases in size and may have central clearing, usually not itchy, hot or painful, typically appearing 1 to 4 weeks after a tick bite (range 3 days to 3 months) and lasting several weeks. Many people do not remember a bite, so its absence does not exclude Lyme. The Scottish Highlands are a recognised area for infected ticks.

points.h: Treat on the rash, no test
points.t: NICE NG95 [1] and QS186 [2]: diagnose and treat Lyme disease without laboratory testing in people with erythema migrans. Serology is often negative early and delays treatment. Testing is for suspected Lyme without erythema migrans.

NICE NG95 [1]: doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days first line for erythema migrans; amoxicillin for 21 days if doxycycline is contraindicated (for example pregnancy), and azithromycin as a further alternative (doses per BNF). BNF: warn about photosensitivity and take with plenty of water, sitting or standing, to avoid oesophageal irritation.

Tinea corporis has a scaly, raised, itchy advancing edge and grows slowly over weeks. Cellulitis is hot, tender, spreading and often with fever. A tick-bite reaction is small, early and does not keep expanding. Size, slow spread, lack of itch and the exposure history point to erythema migrans.

Disseminated Lyme disease can cause facial or other cranial nerve palsy, radicular pain, meningitis (severe headache, neck stiffness), carditis (palpitations, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness, chest pain) and arthritis (a swollen joint, often a knee). These need prompt review; carditis with heart block needs same-day assessment.

UKHSA [3]: cover skin and use repellent in tick areas, check skin after walks, and remove ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers or a tick-removal tool, gripping close to the skin and pulling steadily without crushing, then clean the area. NICE NG95 [1]: do not give antibiotics after a tick bite in a person with no symptoms.

Most people treated early recover fully. Some have tiredness or aches that settle over weeks. If symptoms persist after treatment, review; NICE NG95 [1] allows a second course with an alternative antibiotic and specialist advice when needed.

model.text: Hello Mr Crowther, I’m Dr Patel. How can I help today?

Doc, I got back from a walking holiday in the Highlands about ten days ago and I’ve got this odd rash on my calf. It started small and it’s slowly spread into a big circle, gone a bit clear in the middle, like a target. It’s not that itchy. I wondered if it’s ringworm? I don’t remember any bite.
Thanks, that’s a really clear description. I’d like to ask a few questions, have a look at the rash on the camera, and then we’ll decide together what it is and what to do. Is that okay?
model.why: Agrees an agenda including a remote look at the rash

model.text: Sure.
Could you point the camera at your calf, with something next to it for size, maybe a coin or a ruler?
model.why: Remote examination with a size reference

model.text: Here. It’s about the size of my palm now.
I can see a large round red patch with a paler centre. Is the edge scaly or raised, and is it hot or tender to touch?
Not scaly. Maybe a bit warm, but not sore.
When did you first notice it, and how fast has it grown?
About a week ago. Maybe a bit bigger each day.
On the walk, were you in long grass, bracken, woodland or around deer or sheep?
All of that, really. Long grass most days, and there were deer about.
Have you had fevers, aches, headaches or felt run down? Any drooping of your face, a stiff neck, palpitations or dizzy turns, or a swollen joint?
model.why: Screens for systemic and disseminated features

model.text: Bit tired, maybe achy. Nothing like that otherwise.
Any other rashes elsewhere? Do you take any medicines, have any allergies, or have any reason you couldn’t take an antibiotic?
Just this one. No medicines, no allergies that I know of.
You wondered about ringworm. Was anything else on your mind?
model.why: Explores the idea and hidden concerns

model.text: Honestly, once I searched it, “Lyme disease” came up, and I’ve read horror stories online about people ill for years. I was hoping it was just a fungus and I could get a cream.
That’s a very natural worry, and I’m glad you’ve said it. Let me tell you what I think, and why the news is actually good.
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and signals a clear answer

model.text: I don’t think this is ringworm. A ringworm patch usually has a scaly, itchy edge. A big, slowly spreading red ring that isn’t very itchy, coming up a week or two after walking through tick country, is the typical rash of early Lyme disease. It’s called erythema migrans. Ticks are tiny, so most people never notice the bite.
model.why: Names erythema migrans and explains the discriminating features

model.text: So you think it is Lyme? Don’t I need a blood test?

Good question. With this rash, the national guidance says we diagnose and treat it on what we see. Blood tests are often negative this early, so waiting for one would only delay treatment. The good news is that caught at this stage, Lyme disease responds very well to antibiotics, and most people get completely better.
model.why: Clinical diagnosis without serology (NICE NG95) with proportionate reassurance

model.text: That’s a relief. What about the horror stories?
Those usually come from people whose infection wasn’t recognised early. You’re in the best position: we’ve spotted it and we’re treating it now.

I’ll prescribe doxycycline, one tablet twice a day for 21 days. Take it with a full glass of water and stay upright for a while afterwards, as it can irritate the gullet. It also makes skin burn easily in the sun, so cover up or use sunscreen. Try to finish the whole course.
model.why: Doxycycline per NICE NG95 with BNF counselling

model.text: Three weeks. Okay. Should I do anything about the walking?

Keep walking, just be tick-aware. Long trousers tucked into socks, insect repellent, and check your skin when you get home, especially the backs of the knees, groin and waistband. If you find a tick, take it off quickly with fine tweezers or a tick tool, gripping close to the skin and pulling steadily, without squeezing it, then clean the spot.
Good to know.
Can you tell me back the plan, so I know I’ve explained it well?
It’s probably Lyme from a tick I never saw. Doxycycline twice a day for three weeks with water, careful in the sun. No blood test needed. Check for ticks next time.

Perfect. The rash may take a little while to fade. Contact us urgently if one side of your face droops, you get a severe headache or stiff neck, palpitations, dizzy spells or fainting, chest pain or breathlessness, or later a swollen joint. If the rash keeps spreading after a few days of treatment, or you’re not better when the course finishes, book to see me and we’ll review.
model.why: Specific safety-net for disseminated disease and planned review

social.t: Walking is good for health. The aim is tick awareness, not avoiding the countryside.
Online stories about chronic Lyme can drive anxiety. Offer reliable information and a clear plan for what happens if symptoms persist.

legal.t: Check allergies, pregnancy where relevant and interacting medicines before prescribing doxycycline, and document counselling on photosensitivity and how to take it.

professional.t: A skin lesion can often be assessed well on video or with a photo sent to the practice. Record what was seen, with a size reference, and bring the patient in if the image is not clear enough.
Sending serology when erythema migrans is present adds delay and false reassurance. Follow NICE NG95: treat on the rash.

community.t: UKHSA tick awareness materials cover prevention and safe removal. Countryside and walking organisations often share them for walkers.

redFlags: Facial or other cranial nerve palsy
Palpitations, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness or chest pain (carditis)
Multiple rashes or a rash still spreading on treatment
psychosocial: Worry from online stories about chronic Lyme
Hobby walker likely to be exposed again
ice: Idea: ringworm; no bite, so not from the trip

playbook.diagnosis: “This is erythema migrans, the rash of early Lyme disease, caught from a tick bite you didn’t notice. We diagnose it on the rash and treat it straight away.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A tiny tick, smaller than a poppy seed, can pass on a germ when it bites. The germ spreads out slowly in the skin, which is why the red ring keeps getting bigger with a paler middle. Antibiotics clear it.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought ringworm and hoped for a cream, and you were worried by the stories online. It’s Lyme, but the early, very treatable kind.”
management.psychosocial: Reassure honestly about prognosis; keep him walking safely; give a clear route back if symptoms persist.
sharedPlan: Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days (NICE NG95); with water, upright, sun protection (BNF)
No serology while erythema migrans is present
safetyNet: Facial droop, severe headache or stiff neck, palpitations, dizziness or fainting, chest pain: urgent review
Rash still spreading after a few days of treatment, or symptoms after the course: review

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you recognise erythema migrans and treat it on the rash. Many candidates accept the patient’s ringworm label, or order a Lyme test and wait.

items.fail: Agreeing it is ringworm and prescribing an antifungal.
items.why: Erythema migrans is expanding, usually not itchy or scaly, and follows tick exposure. Missing it delays treatment.
items.fix: Ask about the edge, itch, timing and where he walked.

items.fail: Sending serology and waiting to treat.
items.why: NICE NG95: diagnose and treat without laboratory testing when erythema migrans is present. Early serology is often negative.
items.fix: “With this rash, I treat today, no blood test needed.”

items.fail: Ruling out Lyme because he does not remember a bite.
items.why: Many patients never notice the tick.

items.fail: Wrong antibiotic course, or no counselling.
items.why: NICE NG95: doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days first line. Photosensitivity and oesophageal irritation are common avoidable problems (BNF).
items.fix: Give the full regimen and how to take it.

items.fail: Ignoring or amplifying his fear from online stories.
items.why: Unaddressed anxiety undermines trust; catastrophising is inaccurate for early treated disease.
items.fix: Ask what he has read, then give the honest, good prognosis.

items.why: The later features of Lyme disease are specific and time-critical, such as carditis and facial palsy.
items.fix: Name facial droop, severe headache, palpitations, fainting and joint swelling.

timeMap.d: Let him describe the target rash and the trip. Agree to look on camera.
Size with a reference, edge, scale, warmth, timing, habitat exposure, systemic and disseminated features, allergies.
Ringworm idea, fear from Lyme stories online, hope for a cream.
Erythema migrans; diagnosed on the rash; no blood test; good outlook when treated early.
Doxycycline 21 days with counselling; tick prevention and removal; teach-back; safety-net and review.

wordPics.fail: Diagnoses ringworm and prescribes an antifungal; or suspects Lyme but sends blood tests and waits for results before treating; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises erythema migrans, treats with doxycycline without testing, and gives basic tick advice and a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uses the camera well with a size reference; explains the discriminating features against tinea and cellulitis; gives the correct NG95 regimen with BNF counselling; responds to the online horror stories honestly and proportionately; safety-nets facial palsy, meningism, carditis and arthritis specifically.

avoid.dont: “It looks like ringworm, try an antifungal cream.”
avoid.instead: “A big spreading ring that isn’t itchy, after walking in tick country, is typical of early Lyme disease.”
avoid.why: Mislabelling erythema migrans delays treatment and risks disseminated disease.

avoid.dont: “Let’s do a Lyme blood test and treat if it comes back positive.”
avoid.instead: “With this rash we diagnose and treat straight away. Blood tests are often negative this early.”
avoid.why: NICE NG95 advises treatment without testing when erythema migrans is present.

avoid.dont: “Lyme disease can be really serious and hard to treat.”
avoid.instead: “Caught at this stage it responds very well to antibiotics, and most people recover fully.”
avoid.why: Proportionate, accurate reassurance reduces anxiety and supports adherence.

points.h: Treat on the rash, no test
points.t: NICE NG95 [1] and QS186 [2]: diagnose and treat Lyme disease without laboratory testing in people with erythema migrans. Serology is often negative early and delays treatment. Testing is for suspected Lyme without erythema migrans.

NICE NG95 [1]: doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days first line for erythema migrans; amoxicillin for 21 days if doxycycline is contraindicated (for example pregnancy), and azithromycin as a further alternative (doses per BNF). BNF: warn about photosensitivity and take with plenty of water, sitting or standing, to avoid oesophageal irritation.

Tinea corporis has a scaly, raised, itchy advancing edge and grows slowly over weeks. Cellulitis is hot, tender, spreading and often with fever. A tick-bite reaction is small, early and does not keep expanding. Size, slow spread, lack of itch and the exposure history point to erythema migrans.

Disseminated Lyme disease can cause facial or other cranial nerve palsy, radicular pain, meningitis (severe headache, neck stiffness), carditis (palpitations, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness, chest pain) and arthritis (a swollen joint, often a knee). These need prompt review; carditis with heart block needs same-day assessment.

UKHSA [3]: cover skin and use repellent in tick areas, check skin after walks, and remove ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers or a tick-removal tool, gripping close to the skin and pulling steadily without crushing, then clean the area. NICE NG95 [1]: do not give antibiotics after a tick bite in a person with no symptoms.

Most people treated early recover fully. Some have tiredness or aches that settle over weeks. If symptoms persist after treatment, review; NICE NG95 [1] allows a second course with an alternative antibiotic and specialist advice when needed.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; let him describe the rash and the trip fully before questions.
Walking hobby and future exposure; online stories feeding worry; practical ability to take a 21-day course.
Picked up “I don’t remember any bite” and the Highlands trip and explored both.
Idea (ringworm), concern (Lyme “horror stories”), expectation (an antifungal cream).
Remote look at the rash with a size reference; edge, scale, warmth, tenderness; no blood test needed with erythema migrans.
Erythema migrans versus tinea, cellulitis, tick-bite reaction and insect bite.
Asked about facial palsy, meningism, palpitations, dizziness, fainting, joint swelling and systemic illness.
Named erythema migrans as early Lyme disease and explained why no test is needed.
Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days (NICE NG95) with BNF counselling; allergy and contraindications checked.
Tick prevention and removal advice; encouraged to keep walking safely; supported his worry with a clear plan if symptoms persist.
Teach-back; red flags for disseminated disease; review if the rash spreads on treatment or symptoms persist.

social.t: Walking is good for health. The aim is tick awareness, not avoiding the countryside.
Online stories about chronic Lyme can drive anxiety. Offer reliable information and a clear plan for what happens if symptoms persist.

legal.t: Check allergies, pregnancy where relevant and interacting medicines before prescribing doxycycline, and document counselling on photosensitivity and how to take it.

professional.t: A skin lesion can often be assessed well on video or with a photo sent to the practice. Record what was seen, with a size reference, and bring the patient in if the image is not clear enough.
Sending serology when erythema migrans is present adds delay and false reassurance. Follow NICE NG95: treat on the rash.

community.t: UKHSA tick awareness materials cover prevention and safe removal. Countryside and walking organisations often share them for walkers.

redFlags: Facial or other cranial nerve palsy
Palpitations, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness or chest pain (carditis)
Multiple rashes or a rash still spreading on treatment
psychosocial: Worry from online stories about chronic Lyme
Hobby walker likely to be exposed again
ice: Idea: ringworm; no bite, so not from the trip

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is erythema migrans, the rash of early Lyme disease, caught from a tick bite you didn’t notice. We diagnose it on the rash and treat it straight away.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A tiny tick, smaller than a poppy seed, can pass on a germ when it bites. The germ spreads out slowly in the skin, which is why the red ring keeps getting bigger with a paler middle. Antibiotics clear it.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought ringworm and hoped for a cream, and you were worried by the stories online. It’s Lyme, but the early, very treatable kind.”
management.psychosocial: Reassure honestly about prognosis; keep him walking safely; give a clear route back if symptoms persist.
sharedPlan: Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days (NICE NG95); with water, upright, sun protection (BNF)
No serology while erythema migrans is present
safetyNet: Facial droop, severe headache or stiff neck, palpitations, dizziness or fainting, chest pain: urgent review
Rash still spreading after a few days of treatment, or symptoms after the course: review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you recognise erythema migrans and treat it on the rash. Many candidates accept the patient’s ringworm label, or order a Lyme test and wait.

items.fail: Agreeing it is ringworm and prescribing an antifungal.
items.why: Erythema migrans is expanding, usually not itchy or scaly, and follows tick exposure. Missing it delays treatment.
items.fix: Ask about the edge, itch, timing and where he walked.

items.fail: Sending serology and waiting to treat.
items.why: NICE NG95: diagnose and treat without laboratory testing when erythema migrans is present. Early serology is often negative.
items.fix: “With this rash, I treat today, no blood test needed.”

items.fail: Ruling out Lyme because he does not remember a bite.
items.why: Many patients never notice the tick.

items.fail: Wrong antibiotic course, or no counselling.
items.why: NICE NG95: doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 21 days first line. Photosensitivity and oesophageal irritation are common avoidable problems (BNF).
items.fix: Give the full regimen and how to take it.

items.fail: Ignoring or amplifying his fear from online stories.
items.why: Unaddressed anxiety undermines trust; catastrophising is inaccurate for early treated disease.
items.fix: Ask what he has read, then give the honest, good prognosis.

items.why: The later features of Lyme disease are specific and time-critical, such as carditis and facial palsy.
items.fix: Name facial droop, severe headache, palpitations, fainting and joint swelling.
